original_question: The existence of one hyperbolic prime closed geodesic on a Finsler S^2 implies the existence of infinitely many distinct prime closed geodesics.
target_in_paper: Conjecture 2.2.2 (Long) in §2.2, “Finsler metrics on S^2”: the paper states, in essentially the same words as your draft, that the existence of one hyperbolic prime closed geodesic on a Finsler S^2 should force the existence of infinitely many distinct prime closed geodesics. ([aimath.org](https://aimath.org/pastworkshops/geodesicsproblems.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft is already very close to the paper’s exact target: it has the right ambient object (a Finsler 2-sphere), the right hypothesis (existence of one hyperbolic prime closed geodesic), and the right conclusion (infinitely many distinct prime closed geodesics). It also correctly focuses on the narrower conjecture the paper isolates, rather than drifting to the broader neighboring statement that an irreversible Finsler metric on S^2 has either exactly 2 or infinitely many distinct prime closed geodesics. ([aimath.org](https://aimath.org/pastworkshops/geodesicsproblems.pdf))
missing_details: The paper presents this as a conjecture/open problem, not as a theorem. ([aimath.org](https://aimath.org/pastworkshops/geodesicsproblems.pdf))

To make it fully stand-alone, the universal quantifier should be explicit: for any Finsler metric F on S^2, if (S^2, F) admits one hyperbolic prime closed geodesic, then it should admit infinitely many distinct prime closed geodesics. ([aimath.org](https://aimath.org/pastworkshops/geodesicsproblems.pdf))

The scope should remain exactly all Finsler metrics on S^2; the paper does not restrict Conjecture 2.2.2 to irreversible metrics, reversible metrics, or bumpy metrics. The irreversibility and bumpiness conditions appear only in nearby supporting results, not in the conjecture itself. ([aimath.org](https://aimath.org/pastworkshops/geodesicsproblems.pdf))

The draft leaves the standard term “prime” implicit; in the survey this term is used but not redefined in §2.2, so a stand-alone version should at least preserve that prime closed geodesics are the relevant objects, rather than arbitrary iterates. ([aimath.org](https://aimath.org/pastworkshops/geodesicsproblems.pdf))

The draft also leaves “hyperbolic” implicit; the survey uses the standard dynamical term without restating its definition in §2.2, so a stand-alone version should keep that exact qualifier rather than weakening it to a generic non-elliptic or nondegenerate assumption. ([aimath.org](https://aimath.org/pastworkshops/geodesicsproblems.pdf))

There are no algebraic ambient-ring/field data, degree conditions, homogeneity requirements, nilpotency assumptions, or asymptotic qualifiers in this paper’s statement; the only material implicit data are the quantifier over Finsler metrics on S^2 and the standard meanings of “hyperbolic” and “prime.” ([aimath.org](https://aimath.org/pastworkshops/geodesicsproblems.pdf))
refined_question: Conjecture 2.2.2 (Long). Let F be a Finsler metric on S^2. If (S^2, F) admits a hyperbolic prime closed geodesic, must it admit infinitely many distinct prime closed geodesics? ([aimath.org](https://aimath.org/pastworkshops/geodesicsproblems.pdf))
justification: The draft is targeting the paper’s exact official formulation in §2.2, namely Conjecture 2.2.2 (Long), and not the broader neighboring Conjecture 2.2.1. The surrounding discussion first recalls Bangert–Long’s result that every irreversible Finsler metric on S^2 has at least two distinct prime closed geodesics, then states the broader “exactly 2 or infinitely many” conjecture, and then singles out your target conjecture about a single hyperbolic prime closed geodesic implying infinitely many distinct prime closed geodesics. Immediately afterward, the paper places this next to Conjecture 2.2.3 on elliptic prime closed geodesics and notes supporting evidence coming from Hofer–Wysocki–Zehnder for bumpy Finsler metrics under a transversality condition on stable and unstable manifolds of hyperbolic closed geodesics. The paper does not state any equivalent reformulation of Conjecture 2.2.2. ([aimath.org](https://aimath.org/pastworkshops/geodesicsproblems.pdf))
